blocks.title: How to study
blocks.text: Start with a chapter’s learning goals, then read one teaching page at a time. Follow the diagram or worked example. Pause at the question before moving on, and write an answer in your own notes. Then try the matching chapter mission in the activity section beginning on page 97. Explained answers follow the six missions.

blocks.title: Find a page quickly
blocks.text: This PDF has bookmarks for every chapter and teaching page. Page numbers match the PDF viewer, including the unchanged cover and chapter dividers. The learning goals are on pages 3–4. Missions, optional resources and the complete answer key follow page 96; their bookmarks provide direct navigation. GitHub links are supplementary.

blocks.title: 01 · The Fundamentals
blocks.text: Represent numbers, characters, images and sound; explain stored programs, registers and the fetch–execute cycle; compare translators; describe operating-system tasks, utilities, interrupts and peripheral connections.

blocks.title: 02 · Behaviorism & Behaviorist AI
blocks.text: Distinguish classical and operant conditioning; identify stimulus–response rules and layered robotics; explain reinforcement-learning components, policies, values and exploration; interpret a Q update and the parts of an MDP.

blocks.title: 03 · Hardware
blocks.text: Classify hardware; compare memory and storage; explain processors, pipelining, parallelism and interrupts; connect sensors, converters and actuators; reason with logic gates; evaluate embedded systems, interfaces and AI accelerators.

blocks.title: 04 · Networking
blocks.text: Compare network architectures, clients and clouds; identify communication hardware and media; trace URLs, DNS and TCP/IP; explain application protocols, switching and network performance; distinguish data protection goals, encryption, signatures and TLS.

blocks.title: 05 · Applications
blocks.text: Trace an integrated smart-system workflow; explain real-time deadlines and edge/cloud choices; connect policies to actuators; evaluate automation, human-AI interaction, ethical concerns and connected applications.

blocks.title: 06 · Strengths & Limitations
blocks.text: Evaluate physical and network constraints; distinguish scalability, interoperability and resilience; compare predictive analytics with behavioural modelling; assess resource allocation, explainability, bias and responsible deployment.

blocks.title: Two states, many meanings
blocks.text: A bit is a binary digit: 0 or 1. Electronic circuits distinguish two ranges of voltage, allowing hardware to store and process bits reliably. Eight bits form one byte. A word is the group of bits a processor handles as a unit; its size depends on the architecture. The same pattern may represent a number, a character or an instruction: the interpretation supplies the meaning.

blocks.title: Units matter
blocks.text: Lowercase b means bit; uppercase B means byte. Divide bits by 8 to obtain bytes. Decimal prefixes use powers of ten; binary prefixes use powers of two. For example, 2 KiB = 2 × 1,024 = 2,048 bytes. A network speed in Mb/s is not the same unit as a file size in MB.

blocks.title: Place value does the work
blocks.text: Denary uses powers of 10. Binary uses powers of 2, so the positions in an eight-bit number are 128, 64, 32, 16, 8, 4, 2 and 1. Add the positions containing 1: 00101101 = 32 + 8 + 4 + 1 = 45. To convert denary to binary, select those powers of two, or repeatedly divide by 2 and read the remainders backwards.

blocks.title: Why engineers use hexadecimal
blocks.text: Group binary digits in fours from the right: 0010 1101 becomes 2D. Hexadecimal is a compact notation for the same value, useful in memory dumps, colour codes and hardware addresses. Binary addition carries when a column reaches 2: 1 + 1 = 10. With a fixed width, check whether a carry or signed overflow changes the interpretation.

blocks.title: Read two’s complement
blocks.text: The leftmost bit has a negative weight. In eight bits, 11111011 means −128 + 64 + 32 + 16 + 8 + 2 + 1 = −5. In n bits, the range is −2^(n−1) to 2^(n−1) − 1. Always state the width: a bit pattern has no unique signed meaning without a representation and a width.

blocks.title: Subtract by adding the negative
blocks.text: To calculate 9 − 3 in eight bits, add 00001001 to the two’s complement of 00000011: 11111101. Keep the eight result bits, giving 00000110. A carry outside the width is discarded. Signed overflow occurs when the true result lies outside the representable range; it is not the same as an unsigned carry.

blocks.title: BCD stores one decimal digit at a time
blocks.text: Binary-coded decimal allocates four bits to each decimal digit. Decimal 259 becomes 0010 0101 1001. This is different from converting the whole number 259 to ordinary binary. Patterns 1010–1111 are unused as decimal digits in ordinary BCD. Decimal representations are useful where exact decimal digits matter, including displays and some financial calculations.

blocks.title: Characters need an agreed code
blocks.text: A character set defines the available characters. An encoding maps characters to stored values. ASCII defines 128 codes, covering English letters, digits, punctuation and control characters. Unicode assigns code points to characters from many writing systems. UTF-8 and UTF-16 are ways to encode those code points; Unicode does not mean every character occupies the same number of bytes.

blocks.title: One pattern, different interpretations
blocks.caption: An application must know the agreed format before it can interpret stored data.

blocks.title: Pixels and colour depth
blocks.text: A bitmap is a grid of pixels. Pixel dimensions describe its width and height; resolution may also describe pixel density when an image is displayed or printed. Colour depth is the number of bits used per pixel. With b bits per pixel, up to 2^b different codes are available. More pixels preserve finer spatial detail; more bits per pixel allow more colour or intensity values.

blocks.title: Bitmap versus vector
blocks.text: A vector image stores shapes, paths and their properties. It can scale without pixelation, making it useful for diagrams and logos. Photographs are normally bitmaps. The size formula above excludes headers, palettes, metadata and compression; an actual file may have a different size.

blocks.title: Turn an analogue wave into numbers
blocks.text: An analogue-to-digital converter samples a sound signal. Sampling rate is the number of samples per second, in hertz. Sampling resolution, or bit depth, is the number of bits per sample. A higher rate can represent a wider range of frequencies; a greater bit depth provides finer amplitude steps. Both increase uncompressed storage requirements.

blocks.title: Estimate audio size
blocks.text: Uncompressed audio size in bits = sampling rate × bit depth × channels × duration. For 10 seconds of mono audio at 8,000 samples/s and 16 bits/sample: 8,000 × 16 × 1 × 10 = 1,280,000 bits, or 160,000 bytes. Stereo requires two channels.

blocks.title: Choose the right compression
rows: Suitable for programs and exact records.
Useful when smaller media files justify reduced fidelity.

blocks.title: Instructions and data share memory
blocks.text: In the introductory Von Neumann model, memory holds both instructions and data. The CPU fetches instructions, decodes them and performs the required operations. The arithmetic logic unit (ALU) performs calculations and comparisons. The control unit coordinates the operation of the CPU, memory and input/output devices. Registers hold small amounts of immediately needed information.

blocks.title: The main connections
blocks.caption: Address bus: identifies a location. Data bus: carries instructions or values. Control bus: carries signals such as read and write.

blocks.title: Timing and the bottleneck
blocks.text: The system clock coordinates operations. A clock frequency of 3 GHz means three billion clock cycles per second, not necessarily three billion completed instructions. Cache and pipelining reduce some delays, but moving instructions and data through shared resources can still restrict throughput. Real processors extend this simplified model in many ways.

blocks.title: Follow one instruction
rows: Copy the address in PC to MAR.
Read the memory instruction into MDR.
Advance PC to the next instruction address.
Copy the instruction from MDR to CIR.
Decode the operation and its operand.
Execute; store a result or change control flow.

blocks.title: Give each register a job
blocks.text: PC is the program counter: the next instruction address. MAR identifies the memory location being accessed. MDR holds data moving to or from memory. CIR holds the current instruction. ACC is an accumulator for intermediate arithmetic results in this teaching model. A branch instruction may replace the normal next value of PC.

blocks.title: A useful analogy
blocks.text: Think of a recipe: PC marks the next recipe line, MAR selects its location, MDR carries the line, CIR holds the instruction being followed, and ACC is a temporary mixing bowl. In this simplified one-word instruction model PC advances by 1; actual instruction sizes and timing depend on the processor.

blocks.title: Three translator roles
rows: Assembly mnemonics and labels become machine instructions.
Source program becomes another representation, often native code or bytecode.
Runs program operations through a runtime, sometimes using bytecode.

blocks.title: Choose the right level
blocks.text: Machine code contains the instructions a processor executes. Assembly exposes architecture-specific operations and registers. High-level languages offer abstractions such as variables, functions and data structures. They improve portability, but some translation or runtime support is still needed. A language may have both compiled and interpreted implementations.

blocks.title: Trade-offs are implementation-dependent
blocks.text: Ahead-of-time compilation can support fast execution and catch some errors before running. Interpretation can support rapid experimentation and interactive debugging. Many modern systems combine compilation, interpretation and just-in-time compilation. It is too simple to say that all interpreters translate one source line at a time or that all compilers produce a standalone executable.

blocks.title: Teaching assembly: one instruction per address
rows: Put the literal value 3 in ACC.
Add the literal value 4 to ACC.

blocks.title: Watch state change
blocks.text: Start with PC = 100. After LOAD, ACC = 3. After ADD, ACC = 7. STORE copies 7 to address 200; it does not mean “store the number 200”. The # sign denotes an immediate value in this invented teaching notation. The example illustrates execution; it is not the instruction set of a particular real CPU.

blocks.title: Two passes and a helpful editor
blocks.text: A two-pass assembler first builds a table connecting labels to addresses, then uses it to resolve operands and encode instructions. An integrated development environment (IDE) combines editing, syntax highlighting, completion, translation and debugging. Breakpoints and single-stepping let you inspect the changing PC, registers and memory.

blocks.title: Coordinate shared resources
rows: Schedule CPU time and coordinate running programs.
Allocate and protect memory; manage virtual memory.
Use drivers, organise storage and provide I/O services.
Authenticate users and enforce access permissions.

blocks.title: Utilities support maintenance
blocks.text: Backup software creates recoverable copies; test restoration as well as copying. Antivirus checks for known and suspicious malware activity. A formatter prepares a file system and may destroy access to existing data. Repair tools check file-system structures. Compression tools reduce storage or transfer size. Defragmentation helps some hard disks; it is not routine maintenance for SSDs.

blocks.title: Software does not replace hardware
blocks.text: The OS provides a managed interface to physical resources. A program still needs CPU time, working memory and access to its files. Good resource management improves sharing and responsiveness, but it does not remove limits in memory capacity, processing speed or storage performance.

blocks.title: Respond without checking everything constantly
blocks.text: An interrupt requests the processor’s attention. For an enabled interrupt, the processor and operating system preserve the required execution state, transfer control to an interrupt service routine, then restore state and resume. Exact timing and saved registers depend on the architecture. Not every request is handled immediately; priorities and masking affect when it is serviced.

blocks.title: Interrupt service, conceptually
blocks.caption: A timer interrupt helps an OS share CPU time; an input device may interrupt when data becomes available.

blocks.title: Common peripheral connections
rows: Serial data, plug-and-play peripherals; many versions also provide power.
Digital video and audio for a display.

blocks.title: Start with observable behaviour
blocks.text: Behaviourism studies the relationship between observable behaviour and environmental events. A stimulus is a detectable event; a response is an observable reaction. Pavlov, Watson and Skinner contributed to different strands of this tradition. The approach helped make learning measurable, although it is not a complete description of every kind of human learning.

blocks.title: Two kinds of conditioning
rows: A cue becomes associated with another stimulus.
An action becomes associated with its consequences.
A bell paired with food can trigger salivation.
Sitting followed by a treat can become more frequent.
Focus: behaviour shaped by reinforcement or punishment.

blocks.title: Connect the analogy carefully
blocks.text: Reinforcement learning borrows the idea of learning from consequences, but an algorithm is not a human or animal mind. A numerical reward is a training signal. It does not imply feelings, understanding or consciousness. Use the analogy to identify a feedback relationship, then describe the computational mechanism precisely.

blocks.title: A sensor can trigger a useful action
blocks.text: A simple robotic vacuum may move forward until a bumper is pressed, then reverse and turn. Its environment is the room, its stimulus is the bumper signal, and its response is the movement. These rules can produce useful behaviour without a detailed map. If the rules never change from experience, this is reactive control rather than reinforcement learning.

blocks.title: A direct feedback path
blocks.caption: Situated systems act in an environment; embodied systems have a physical body that constrains and enables action.

blocks.title: Layers and priorities
blocks.text: Brooks’ subsumption architecture coordinates relatively simple behaviour modules. A module can inhibit or suppress another module’s output under specified conditions. A designer might combine wandering, obstacle avoidance and task seeking while protecting a safety stop. This is one design approach, not a claim that all map-based planning is slow or unreliable; practical robots often combine reactive control and planning.

blocks.title: Learn a policy through experience
blocks.text: Reinforcement learning is a way for an agent to learn decisions through interaction. The agent observes a state or observation, selects an action, and receives feedback from the environment. A learning algorithm uses that experience to improve a policy: the rule or strategy for choosing actions. The objective is usually expected cumulative reward, not just the next reward.

blocks.title: One interaction at time t
blocks.caption: Repeat: observe, act, receive feedback, then update. The learning update may occur during training rather than every deployed action.

blocks.title: Name the components
rows: A simulated rover / a grid with obstacles.
Current square / move up, down, left or right.
Points for outcomes / a strategy for selecting moves.

blocks.title: Feedback evaluates an outcome
blocks.text: A reward is a numerical signal associated with an interaction. It may be positive, zero or negative. A reward of −1 is not a moral judgement: its role is defined by the task. Designers might reward reaching a goal, penalise a collision and charge a small cost per step. Poorly chosen rewards can encourage shortcuts that defeat the intended goal.

blocks.title: Distinguish the three ideas
blocks.text: The reward says how an outcome scores now. A policy says what action to choose in a situation. A value estimate says how much future reward is expected from a state or a state–action choice. A good policy may accept a small immediate cost to achieve a larger long-term return. Q-learning estimates action values and derives choices from them.

blocks.title: The learning question
blocks.caption: A fixed rule such as “if hot, turn on fan” may control a system effectively without learning any values or changing a policy.

blocks.title: Use the restaurant analogy
blocks.text: Exploitation is ordering a dish you already believe is best. Exploration is trying another dish to learn more about it. In an RL task, exploitation chooses the action with the best current value estimate, including future return. Exploration gathers information about other actions. Early estimates can be wrong, so always exploiting can lock an agent into an inferior policy.

blocks.title: An epsilon-greedy example
rows: With 10% probability, choose a random permitted action.
Otherwise choose an action with the highest current Q value.
Measure outcomes and update estimates; epsilon may change over time.

blocks.title: Think before choosing
blocks.text: Suppose one route has worked twice and another has never been tried. Is the first route certainly better? No: evidence is incomplete. Exploration can improve knowledge, but it also has a cost. In physical systems, experiments must respect safety constraints; training in a simulation does not automatically make every real-world action safe.

blocks.title: A table of learned action values
blocks.text: Q(s, a) estimates the return from taking action a in state s and then following a good policy. Q-learning is model-free: it learns from transitions without needing a supplied transition model. “Model-free” does not mean memory-free or that the agent lacks a table or neural network.

blocks.title: The update rule
blocks.text: Q(new) = Q(old) + alpha × [reward + gamma × max Q(next state, next action) − Q(old)]. Alpha controls the size of an update. Gamma discounts future rewards. The quantity in square brackets is the temporal-difference error. For a terminal next state, use zero for the future-value term.

blocks.title: Interpret the result
blocks.text: This experience raised the estimate from 2 to 3.3. It did not prove the action is always best. Repeated experience, an appropriate learning schedule and sufficient exploration are important; one reward does not establish a reliable policy.

title: A decision problem as an MDP

blocks.title: Five parts of a Markov decision process
rows: Transition probabilities: where an action can lead.
Reward function: how outcomes are scored.
Discount factor: how future rewards are weighted.

blocks.title: The Markov property
blocks.text: A state is Markov when it contains the information needed to predict the next-state and reward distribution, given the current action. Earlier history adds no further predictive information once that state is known. A position alone may be insufficient: a robot may also need speed, battery level or whether it is carrying a package.

blocks.title: Observation is not always state
blocks.text: Sensors can provide incomplete or noisy observations. A camera view may hide an obstacle or omit velocity. An agent may need memory or a state estimate to work with partial information. A simple grid world is useful because we can explicitly specify the state, actions, transitions and rewards instead of assuming the agent knows everything.

blocks.title: A slippery grid square
blocks.text: Imagine an agent choosing “forward”. In this illustrative environment, it reaches the intended square with probability 0.8 and slips sideways with probability 0.2. The action is chosen by the agent; the transition outcome is sampled by the environment. The probabilities for all possible next outcomes must sum to 1.

blocks.title: One action, two outcomes
blocks.caption: For immediate rewards of +10 and −5, the expected immediate reward is 0.8 × 10 + 0.2 × (−5) = 7. Future rewards may change which action is best.

blocks.title: Expected is not guaranteed
blocks.text: An expected value of 7 does not mean every attempt earns 7. It summarises the average implied by the model. A system that learns under one set of transition probabilities may perform poorly when its environment changes. Test across plausible conditions rather than judging a policy from a single successful run.

title: Training is different from using a policy

blocks.title: Separate two phases
blocks.text: During training, the system collects experience and updates estimates or policy parameters. During deployment, it may use a fixed learned policy without further learning. Some applications allow controlled online updates, but adaptation is not automatic. A robot can react to a new sensor reading while keeping exactly the same policy.

blocks.title: Test what was actually learned
blocks.text: Check whether success persists with different starting states, sensor noise and changed conditions. Compare against a simple fixed-rule baseline. Examine failure cases as well as average reward. If the goal is “arrive safely”, a reward that only measures speed may produce an undesirable strategy even when the algorithm is working as specified.

blocks.title: A responsible learning workflow
blocks.caption: Behaviour-based robotics, reinforcement learning and neural networks are related ideas, not interchangeable labels. A system can use one without using all three.

Layered behaviour coordination using suppression or inhibition.
The decision-maker / the system it interacts with.
A representation sufficient for a task / the information actually sensed.

A strategy that maps a situation to action choices.

blocks.title: Classify by the job being performed
blocks.text: Hardware is the physical part of a computer system. An input device supplies data, a processing device transforms it, an output device communicates or acts on a result, and storage retains information. One device can have several roles: a touchscreen displays output and senses input. A barcode reader is input; an SSD is storage.

blocks.title: From a physical event to a response
blocks.caption: The processor follows instructions. Useful behaviour depends on the program, the data, the hardware and their connections.

blocks.title: How hardware enables AI
blocks.text: An AI model must run as computations on hardware. Sensors provide observations, memory holds model parameters and working data, a processor evaluates the model, and an output device communicates the decision. A physical robot also needs a powered actuator to move. More powerful hardware can increase capacity or speed, but does not itself create a learning algorithm.

blocks.title: A useful hierarchy
rows: Very small, very fast storage inside the processor.
Fast memory holding copies of recently or frequently used data.
Working storage for active programs and data; normally volatile.
Larger, persistent storage; usually slower to access.

blocks.title: SRAM and DRAM
blocks.text: Static RAM stores bits using bistable circuits such as flip-flops. It needs power but no periodic refresh, and is commonly used for CPU caches. Dynamic RAM stores charge in cells that must be refreshed; its greater density and lower cost make it suitable for main memory. Both are volatile. Cache can be on the processor chip; it is not necessarily external.

blocks.title: Why an AI workload needs memory
blocks.text: Model weights, input data and intermediate results must fit somewhere. A fast processor can spend time waiting for data if memory bandwidth is insufficient. Capacity answers “how much fits?” Bandwidth answers “how quickly can it move?” These are different constraints and both affect performance.

title: Keep data when power is off

blocks.title: ROM and flash families
rows: Erased with ultraviolet light, then reprogrammed.
Electrically erasable memory, normally erased in blocks.

blocks.title: Magnetic, solid-state and optical media
blocks.text: A hard disk stores data magnetically on rotating platters. Seek time and rotational latency delay access; fragmentation can increase head movement. An SSD stores data in flash with no moving parts. It avoids mechanical seek and rotation delays, but still has nonzero access latency and finite write endurance. External drives can provide portable backup storage.

blocks.title: Optical storage
blocks.text: CDs, DVDs and Blu-ray discs use laser light to read recorded features. Some discs have multiple recording layers. Material defects and optical effects, including birefringence, can disrupt reading. Choose a medium using capacity, access time, cost, durability and the need for long-term retention rather than assuming one technology is best for every purpose.

blocks.title: Introductory design tendencies
rows: Can include more complex and variable-length instructions.
Typically separates loads/stores from register arithmetic.
May allow operations with memory operands.
Examples include ARM and RISC-V families.
A major example is the x86 family.

blocks.title: The distinction is not a speed guarantee
blocks.text: A reduced instruction set does not guarantee that every instruction takes one clock cycle. A complex instruction set does not prevent pipelining or high performance. Modern processors use caches, pipelines, prediction and other techniques; many translate instructions internally into simpler operations. Some RISC families also support compressed instruction encodings.

blocks.title: Look at the workload
blocks.text: Performance depends on implementation, clock frequency, instructions per cycle, memory behaviour, software and energy constraints. A mobile device may prioritise power efficiency; a workstation may prioritise throughput. Compare measured work done under relevant conditions instead of judging a CPU from the RISC or CISC label alone.

blocks.title: Use the laundry analogy
blocks.text: A laundry can wash one load while drying an earlier load. Similarly, a processor pipeline can fetch a new instruction while decoding or executing previous ones. This increases throughput after the pipeline fills; it does not necessarily reduce the latency of an individual instruction. Pipelining is used in both RISC and CISC implementations.

blocks.title: Why a pipeline can pause
blocks.text: A data hazard occurs when an instruction needs a result that is not ready. A control hazard occurs when a branch makes the next instruction uncertain. A structural hazard occurs when operations need the same resource. Stalling, forwarding, scheduling and prediction can help, depending on the processor. “Overlapping” does not mean every instruction is independent.

blocks.title: Flynn’s classification
rows: One instruction stream processes individual data.
One operation applied to many array elements.
Rare; different processing of one data stream.
Independent cores or computers run different work.

blocks.title: Scale beyond one processor
blocks.text: A cluster connects computers, called nodes, so they can coordinate work. Massively parallel systems distribute large tasks across many processing units. Supercomputers are designed for demanding scientific or engineering computation; they are not simply a synonym for mainframes. Communication, synchronisation and data movement affect whether adding processors actually helps.

blocks.title: Connect this to AI
blocks.text: Large arrays of multiplications can benefit from parallel hardware. Parts of an AI workload may still be sequential or limited by memory and communication. A GPU has its own execution model, often described using SIMT, and provides SIMD-like parallel arithmetic; the simple taxonomy is a starting point, not a complete description of every chip.

blocks.title: Events can change the schedule
blocks.text: A sensor, network interface or timer can raise an interrupt. The CPU responds when the request is enabled and eligible. It preserves enough context to resume the interrupted work and transfers execution to a handler. The handler deals with the event and returns. The hardware and operating system divide the responsibility for saving and restoring state.

blocks.title: A simplified service sequence
blocks.caption: Context can include the program counter, status and required registers. Exact details vary by architecture.

blocks.title: Predictability matters
blocks.text: A system with a timing deadline must account for interrupt priority, handler execution time and other sources of delay. RISC versus CISC alone does not determine interrupt latency. Long or frequent interrupt handling can delay useful work. A well-designed system measures worst-case behaviour rather than assuming every event will receive an immediate response.

blocks.title: Gates transform binary signals
blocks.text: AND produces 1 only when all inputs are 1. OR produces 1 when at least one input is 1. NOT inverts one input. XOR produces 1 when two inputs differ. NAND is the inverse of AND; NOR is the inverse of OR. A truth table lists every possible input combination and its corresponding output.

blocks.title: Read symbols and conditions
blocks.text: NOT maps 0 to 1 and 1 to 0. An AND symbol has a flat input side and curved output side; an OR symbol has a curved input side and pointed output. A small output circle means inversion. In a control rule, “door closed AND start pressed” requires both conditions; “smoke OR manual alarm” requires either.

blocks.title: Useful identities
rows: A AND 1 = A; A OR 0 = A
A AND A = A; A OR A = A
A AND NOT A = 0; A OR NOT A = 1
NOT(A AND B) = (NOT A) OR (NOT B)
NOT(A OR B) = (NOT A) AND (NOT B)

blocks.title: A worked simplification
blocks.text: Let X = (A AND B) OR (A AND NOT B). Factor out A: X = A AND (B OR NOT B). The term in brackets is always 1, so X = A AND 1 = A. A simpler equivalent circuit can reduce hardware and delay. Check equivalence by comparing truth-table outputs for every input combination.

blocks.title: Keep the negation in the right place
blocks.text: De Morgan’s laws negate the whole grouped expression on the left. Dropping that outer NOT changes the meaning. Parentheses make the scope clear, especially when a printed overbar is difficult to see. In Boolean algebra, OR is not ordinary arithmetic addition: 1 OR 1 is still 1.

blocks.title: Monitoring versus control
blocks.text: A monitoring system records or displays measurements. A control system also acts on the environment. In a greenhouse, a temperature sensor supplies a reading, a processor compares it with a target, and a fan changes the temperature. A later measurement closes the feedback loop. This can be a fixed-rule controller; learning is not required.

blocks.title: An environmental control loop
blocks.caption: The changed environment is measured again. Analogue sensors may need an ADC; many sensors already provide digital data.

blocks.title: Signals are not actuator power
blocks.text: An ADC converts an analogue signal to a digital value. A DAC converts a digital value to an analogue signal. Some actuators use PWM or digital interfaces instead of a DAC. PWM is a timed switching signal, not the same thing as analogue conversion. A motor driver or power stage supplies the current needed to move a motor or operate a valve.

blocks.title: A dedicated purpose
blocks.text: An embedded system performs a particular role within a larger product, such as a washing-machine controller or a sensor node. A microcontroller typically combines a CPU, memory and input/output peripherals on one chip. An embedded system may use a microcontroller, a larger processor or specialised hardware, depending on its requirements.

blocks.title: Benefits and constraints
rows: Limited memory, processing capacity and battery energy.
Upgrades and repairs may be difficult.
Timing and reliability must be tested, not assumed.
Local operation without a cloud link.
External data or remote management may still need a network.

blocks.title: Design around the task
blocks.text: A small fixed-rule controller may need only modest hardware. A vision model can require much more memory and computation. Choose sensors, processing capacity, interfaces and power together. Environmental temperature, moisture, vibration and expected service life also influence whether a design is suitable.

title: The hardware behind an AI model

blocks.title: Different processing strengths
rows: General control, branching and diverse program tasks.
High-throughput parallel arithmetic for suitable workloads.
Specialised tensor operations with hardware-specific efficiency.
Hold weights, inputs, intermediate results and saved models.

blocks.title: Training and inference have different costs
blocks.text: Training adjusts model parameters using data or experience. Inference uses a model to produce an output. A model may be trained on a large server and deployed on a smaller device. Simple tabular reinforcement learning can run on an ordinary CPU; AI does not always require a GPU, and a specialised chip is not automatically faster for every workload.

blocks.title: Trace the whole path
blocks.text: For a camera-based robot, the sensor captures an image, memory buffers it, processing estimates a useful state, a policy selects an action, and control hardware drives the actuator. Delays in any stage matter. Model size, memory movement, power consumption and heat can be as important as the advertised arithmetic speed of the chip.

title: Interfaces you can see and touch

blocks.title: Touch and display technologies
rows: Detects changes in an electric field; often supports multi-touch.
Pressure brings conductive layers into contact.
Organic light-emitting pixels produce their own light.
Combines displays, optics and tracking to present an immersive view.

blocks.title: Display quality involves trade-offs
blocks.text: Screen resolution describes pixel dimensions. OLED can provide deep blacks because individual pixels can be off, but power use depends on displayed content and hardware. Capacitive and resistive touch differ in input methods, clarity, durability and cost. A touchscreen is both an input surface and an output display.

blocks.title: Build physical objects layer by layer
blocks.text: In material-extrusion 3D printing, a nozzle deposits material to form successive layers. In binder-based printing, a binder joins selected regions of a powder bed. These are different additive-manufacturing methods; material properties and post-processing requirements differ. A printer turns digital instructions into physical output through controlled motion and material handling.

blocks.title: Build your vocabulary
rows: Data entry / results or action / retention of information.
Loses data without power / retains data without power.
Bistable-cell memory / charge-based memory requiring refresh.
Electrically erasable memory / a block-erasable family.
Fast storage holding copies of data near a processor.
Magnetic disk / solid-state storage / laser-readable media.
Instruction-set design families; not direct performance guarantees.

blocks.title: Chapter 3 · Question 1b

title: Connect a room, a city, a world

blocks.title: What a network provides
blocks.text: A network connects devices so they can exchange data and share services, storage or hardware. A connected device is a node. Networks differ in scale, ownership, transmission media and management. Geographic size alone does not determine speed: a particular WAN link can be faster than a particular local wireless connection.

blocks.title: Names describe the scope
rows: A person’s nearby devices; a WPAN is wireless.
A home, office or building; a WLAN uses wireless links.
A metropolitan area or several sites across a city.
Widely separated sites, regions or countries.

blocks.title: A practical analogy
blocks.text: A personal conversation resembles a PAN, a building intercom resembles a LAN, and an inter-city transport network resembles a WAN. Real networks can contain smaller networks inside them. The Internet is a global interconnection of networks, built from links and equipment operated by many organisations.

blocks.title: Two ways to organise services
rows: Peers can both request and provide resources.
Central management can simplify permissions and backup.
Resources can be distributed among participating peers.
Capacity and resilience require deliberate design.
Coordination and consistent security can be harder.

blocks.title: Servers are roles, not magic boxes
blocks.text: A file server provides access to shared files. One physical machine can host several server programs, and a service can run across many machines. A server failure need not stop an entire network if replication or failover is provided. A small P2P setup can be inexpensive, while large P2P systems can also scale when their protocols are designed for it.

blocks.title: A service request
blocks.caption: A peer may act as a client for one exchange and as a server for another. Describe the role being performed.

blocks.title: Thin and thick clients
rows: Relies heavily on remote applications or services.
Network and server availability affect its main tasks.
Needs suitable local hardware and maintenance.

blocks.title: Public and private clouds
blocks.text: A public cloud provides services using infrastructure operated by a provider for multiple customers. A private cloud is dedicated to one organisation and can be on-site or hosted elsewhere. Public cloud can reduce initial capital cost and offer flexible capacity; private cloud can provide greater direct control but requires resources to manage.

blocks.title: Compare actual responsibilities
blocks.text: Neither deployment is automatically secure. Consider access control, configuration, backups, data location, operational expertise and ongoing cost. Replication improves availability but is not a substitute for a recoverable backup. A thin client still performs some local processing, such as displaying an interface; “thin” does not mean it has no CPU.

title: The devices along a network path

blocks.title: Recognise the job
rows: Connects a host to a network interface.
Forwards frames between LAN ports or segments.
Connects wireless stations to a network.
Repeats signals; a hub sends them to multiple ports.
Translates between systems / modulates and demodulates signals.

blocks.title: Addresses serve different scopes
blocks.text: An Ethernet switch learns which MAC addresses are reachable through which ports. A router uses IP routing information to select a next hop. MAC addresses can be changed or randomised; they are not always permanently fixed identifiers. A modem’s modulation depends on the medium, rather than being limited to old telephone lines.

blocks.title: A switch is selective, not omniscient
blocks.text: Known unicast frames can be sent to a selected port. Broadcasts and unknown destinations may be flooded within the relevant LAN. A router chooses a route using its routing table and policies; it does not always measure the least congested possible path for every packet.

blocks.title: Choose a link for its conditions
blocks.text: Twisted-pair copper reduces some electromagnetic interference by twisting paired conductors. Optical fibre carries light and supports high-capacity links. Wi-Fi uses shared radio channels; Bluetooth connects nearby devices using its own radio protocols. Range, speed and frequency-hopping behaviour depend on the version, equipment and environment, not one universal distance or channel count.

blocks.title: Collision detection and avoidance
rows: Historically used on shared, half-duplex Ethernet.
Used by Wi-Fi to manage shared radio access.
Listen, transmit, detect collision, back off and retry.
Listen, wait/back off, transmit and use acknowledgements.
Modern switched full-duplex Ethernet has no collisions on the link.
RTS/CTS is an optional mechanism, not a compulsory step every time.

blocks.title: Use the conversation analogy
blocks.text: At a busy table, people listen before speaking and pause if they talk over each other. Random backoff reduces repeated clashes. Avoidance reduces the chance of a collision; it cannot guarantee one never happens. Interference, hidden stations and missing acknowledgements can still cause retries and delay.

blocks.title: The web is one Internet service
blocks.text: The Internet carries many kinds of communication. The World Wide Web uses linked resources accessed through web protocols. Email and other services also use the Internet. IPv4 addresses have 32 bits; IPv6 addresses have 128 bits. An address helps identify a network interface for communication, while routing determines how packets are forwarded.

blocks.title: Read a URL: https://example.org:443/course/notes?q=ai#part2
rows: Scheme: how the resource is accessed.
Fragment identifying a location within the resource.

blocks.title: A URL is not just an IP address
blocks.text: The host name may be resolved through DNS. The path selects a resource on that host and need not correspond to a physical directory. Default ports can be omitted. A browser normally handles the fragment locally rather than sending it as part of an HTTP request.

blocks.title: Names are easier to remember
blocks.text: The Domain Name System maps names to records, including records that provide IP addresses. A browser and operating system may already have a cached answer. If not, a recursive resolver can obtain an answer using the DNS hierarchy. Cached answers remain usable for their permitted lifetime, reducing repeat lookups.

blocks.title: A simplified lookup
blocks.caption: The resolver follows referrals, receives the requested record, caches it and returns the answer to the client.

blocks.title: The lookup is only one step
blocks.text: After resolving a host, a client still needs to establish suitable communication with the service. DNS does not deliver the web page itself, and it does not translate an entire URL, including its path, into an address. Failures in DNS, connectivity, transport, security negotiation or the application can each prevent a page from loading.

title: Give each protocol layer a job

blocks.title: The four-layer TCP/IP model
rows: IP addressing and routing between networks.
Local network delivery and access to the medium.

blocks.title: Encapsulation is packaging
blocks.text: Application data is carried inside transport data, which is carried inside IP packets, which are carried by link-layer frames. Each layer has its own fields and scope. A frame’s MAC addresses are not the same thing as an IP packet’s addresses; the frame can change at the next link while the packet continues its journey.

blocks.title: Reliable ordering is a service choice
blocks.text: TCP provides an ordered byte stream with reliability and flow/congestion control. UDP provides datagrams without those guarantees by itself. Applications may build additional mechanisms over UDP. Not every IP packet contains a sequence number that allows a router to rebuild a file: reconstruction belongs to the relevant endpoint protocol.

blocks.title: Identify the application protocol
rows: Web requests and responses; HTTPS protects HTTP using TLS.
Traditional file transfer; plain FTP is not encrypted.
Retrieving email, with retention behaviour set by the client.
Structures message content and attachments; not a transport protocol.

blocks.title: A BitTorrent example
blocks.text: BitTorrent divides a file into pieces that peers exchange. A swarm is the participating group. A seed has the complete content and can upload pieces. A downloading peer may upload too; the word “leecher” does not necessarily mean a malicious user. Trackers can help peers discover one another, while distributed discovery is also possible.

blocks.title: Security is part of the choice
blocks.text: A protocol name alone may not guarantee confidentiality or authenticity. Use protected versions or secure alternatives where appropriate. File-transfer tools such as SFTP use a different protocol from FTP. A networked application must also authenticate users and apply access controls at the service.

title: Reserve a path or share capacity?

blocks.title: Circuit and packet switching
rows: Reserves communication capacity for a session.
Shares links by sending discrete packets.
Uses capacity efficiently across variable traffic.
Reservation can be idle during pauses.
Queues, loss and variable delay need management.

blocks.title: Packets move hop by hop
blocks.text: A sender divides or packages data according to its protocols. Routers forward IP packets using destination information. Packets may follow different routes or arrive out of order, although this is not required for every transfer. Endpoint protocols handle the reliability or ordering their applications need.

blocks.title: Apply the comparison carefully
blocks.text: A reserved circuit still has propagation and processing delay; it does not mean zero latency or perfect reliability. Modern Internet video calls commonly use packet-switched networks, buffering, congestion control and other techniques. The source exercise about a preferred circuit assumes a scenario valuing reserved capacity; it is not a universal description of today’s video conferencing.

blocks.title: Four problems to distinguish
rows: How much data a link can carry per second.
The successful transfer rate actually achieved.
How long a transfer or response takes.

blocks.title: Why a fast link can still feel slow
blocks.text: A wide road carries many cars, but a long journey still takes time. Similarly, high bandwidth does not remove propagation delay, queueing or server processing. Retransmitting lost data can add delay; interference and contention can reduce throughput. Measure the entire task, not just the advertised link rate.

blocks.title: Choose a response to the problem
blocks.text: Compress or summarise data when capacity is limited. Reduce unnecessary round trips when latency matters. Use timestamps to identify stale measurements. Buffering can smooth jitter for playback, but adds delay. Redundancy and reconnect logic can improve resilience, while local control keeps a time-critical action from depending on an unavailable remote link.

blocks.title: Three different goals
rows: Who can access, change or disrupt the system?
How is personal data collected, used and shared?
Has the data remained correct and unaltered?

blocks.title: Validation versus verification
blocks.text: Validation checks whether an input meets rules: range, type, length or a valid calendar date. It cannot prove a plausible value is true. Verification checks that data agrees with a source or expected copy, such as double entry or a transfer checksum. Checksums detect some errors; a cryptographic authentication mechanism is needed to resist deliberate modification by an attacker.

blocks.title: Use layers of protection
blocks.text: Strong authentication, least-privilege access, updates, backups and network filtering address different risks. Malware can damage or steal data; spyware monitors activity; phishing tricks a user; pharming redirects a user to an unintended destination. A firewall is not a substitute for secure software, and antivirus cannot promise to detect every threat.

blocks.title: From plaintext to ciphertext
blocks.text: Encryption uses an algorithm and a key to transform readable plaintext into ciphertext. Correctly implemented cryptography can protect confidentiality, but key management and authentication remain essential. Encryption alone does not prove who sent a message or ensure that a device receiving it is trustworthy.

blocks.title: Two approaches
rows: Uses a related public/private key pair.
Supports mechanisms such as key establishment and signatures.
Both parties must obtain the secret securely.
The public key must be authenticated to its owner.

blocks.title: Combine their strengths
blocks.text: Secure protocols commonly use asymmetric mechanisms to authenticate or establish shared secrets, then symmetric authenticated encryption for application traffic. Keep private keys private. Do not invent an encryption scheme by substituting characters or treating a checksum as a secret; the design and implementation of cryptography require established protocols.

blocks.title: A signature protects authenticity and integrity
blocks.text: A sender signs a message, usually through a hash-based construction, using a private signing key. A verifier checks the signature with the matching public key. A valid signature supports a claim about the key used and whether the signed content changed. It does not encrypt the message or prove that the message’s claims are true.

blocks.title: A simplified verification path
blocks.caption: Signing is not generally “encryption in reverse”; the operations depend on the signature algorithm.

blocks.title: Certificates and TLS
blocks.text: A digital certificate binds an identity, such as a domain name, to a public key and is signed by an issuer. A client checks the trust chain, validity and expected name. TLS uses authentication and cryptography to protect communication, including HTTPS. SSL is obsolete and should not be deployed. A certificate can authenticate a domain without proving the site is honest in every other respect.

blocks.title: Blocks and streams
blocks.text: A block cipher operates on fixed-size blocks; a mode specifies how it is used for longer messages. A stream cipher combines data with a generated keystream. Reusing a key/nonce combination incorrectly can undermine security. Authenticated encryption also detects unauthorised changes, rather than providing confidentiality alone.

blocks.title: Understand CBC as a historical example
blocks.text: Cipher block chaining combines a plaintext block with the previous ciphertext block before encryption, starting with an initialisation vector. Correct IV handling, padding and authentication matter. CBC is useful to understand, but a new application should use a vetted protocol and suitable authenticated-encryption construction rather than assembling its own cryptographic workflow.

blocks.title: What quantum key distribution does
blocks.text: QKD uses quantum signals and classical communication to establish key material. Its security analysis detects disturbance statistically under stated assumptions; it does not make every device or message unhackable. It requires specialised infrastructure and authenticated classical communication. Post-quantum cryptography is a different approach: algorithms designed to resist quantum attacks on conventional computers.

blocks.title: Build your vocabulary
rows: Local / wide-area / metropolitan / personal network scopes.
Service requester / provider / participant that can perform both roles.
Relies more on remote resources / performs substantial local work.
Forwards local frames / forwards IP packets between networks.
A network interface / a wireless network access device.
Communication rules / a layered organisation of those rules.
A link-layer unit / a routed Internet-layer unit.
A resource locator / a distributed name-resolution system.
Ordered reliable byte-stream transport / datagram transport.

blocks.title: Chapter 4 · Question 6c
blocks.text: Name three mechanisms used to protect computer systems against threats.

title: A system that senses and acts

blocks.title: Combine the parts
blocks.text: An integrated smart system connects physical hardware, communication and software to carry out a useful task. Sensors collect information; processing interprets it and selects an output; actuators change the world. A network lets components exchange data or use remote services. Some systems use fixed rules, some use learned models, and some combine both.

blocks.title: Follow one complete workflow
blocks.caption: The changed environment supplies the next observation. The communication step may be local, remote or partly unnecessary for a self-contained controller.

blocks.title: Use the body analogy carefully
blocks.text: Sensors resemble senses, actuators resemble muscles and communication links resemble nerves. Software coordinates the response. This is an analogy for the roles, not a claim that the machine has a human mind. Explain the actual mechanism: what is measured, what message is sent, what computation runs and what physical output follows.

blocks.title: Trace the flow of information
rows: Soil-moisture sensors report readings and timestamps.
A low-power network sends readings to a local gateway.
A controller selects a watering action using targets and constraints.
A driver energises a valve; later readings show the effect.

blocks.title: Add learning only when it has a role
blocks.text: A fixed threshold can open a valve when soil is dry. A learned policy might instead use moisture, recent rain and other state variables to trade off water use and crop needs. Reinforcement learning would require a defined reward and a process for updating the policy from experience. Merely connecting a sensor to Wi-Fi does not make the system learn.

blocks.title: Check assumptions before action
blocks.text: Sensors can drift; messages can arrive late; a valve can fail. Timestamp readings, detect implausible values and monitor the effect of each action. A real deployment needs domain-specific limits and testing. This example explains an architecture rather than prescribing watering durations for a particular crop.

blocks.title: Correctness includes timing
blocks.text: A real-time system must produce the required response within a specified deadline. “Real-time” does not simply mean very fast. Missing a hard deadline can make a system fail its requirements; missing a soft deadline reduces service quality. Batch work, such as a monthly report, usually has different timing needs.

blocks.title: Interpret the calculation correctly
blocks.text: Distance during delay = speed × delay. This is only the distance travelled before a response begins, not total stopping distance. Sensing, processing, communication, actuation and physical braking all contribute to a real system. Moving a critical computation locally removes some communication delay, but it does not guarantee a particular safe outcome.

blocks.title: Separate the fast loop from shared services
blocks.text: A useful architecture keeps time-critical sensing, policy evaluation and actuator control near the device. A network can carry telemetry, coordinate multiple devices or distribute reviewed model updates. Training may occur centrally while a fixed policy runs locally. A system can continue its local task during a link outage only if it was designed to do so.

blocks.title: Two connected responsibilities
blocks.caption: Local action does not have to wait for every cloud exchange. This is an architectural choice, not a property of all AI systems.

blocks.title: Make messages interpretable
blocks.text: Include a device identity, timestamp, sequence number, units and model or policy version where needed. Reject stale or unauthorised commands. Delayed feedback must be associated with the action that produced it before a learning update is made. Network loss can reduce the evidence available for training; it should not silently become a reward of zero.

blocks.title: A spectrum of responsibility
rows: A human performs the task directly.
The system supports selected actions or provides alerts.
The system handles parts of the task; the human supervises.
The system acts within a defined operating domain.

blocks.title: Benefits depend on the setting
blocks.text: Automation can improve repeatability, throughput and availability for suitable work. It can also shift errors from isolated human mistakes to systematic software, sensor or model failures affecting many operations. Do not assume that automation gives zero errors, unlimited uptime or a fixed percentage improvement.

blocks.title: Keep the operating domain explicit
blocks.text: A warehouse robot may work well on a mapped, maintained floor but fail on an unfamiliar surface. A human must understand what the system can handle, what it cannot handle and how a handover works. Formal driving-automation levels describe a specific domain; they should not be treated as a universal ladder for every smart appliance.

blocks.title: Describe the learning mechanism
blocks.text: An RL agent collects transitions: a state, an action, a reward and a next state. A learning algorithm uses those transitions to update values or policy parameters. A positive reward does not mechanically guarantee that an action becomes more likely in every algorithm; updates depend on the method and its estimates of future return.

blocks.title: Design an illustrative delivery task
rows: Location, remaining energy and relevant obstacle information.
Score progress and successful completion; penalise undesirable outcomes.
Disallow unsafe actions even if a reward would favour them.

blocks.title: A deployment may stop learning
blocks.text: A trained policy can be evaluated repeatedly on new observations without changing its parameters. Online learning requires a controlled update process and evidence that changes improve performance. Separate “the action changed because the observation changed” from “the policy changed because the agent learned”.

title: Turn a decision into an action

blocks.title: A command needs an execution path
blocks.caption: Feedback from position, current or other sensors can confirm whether the requested action happened.

blocks.title: Different physical outputs
rows: Rotate a wheel or position a joint.
Open or close a fluid path.

blocks.title: Distinguish information from energy
blocks.text: A software value such as “target angle = 15 degrees” is information. Interface electronics convert it into a suitable control signal; a powered mechanism supplies the force. Some systems use analogue voltages, others PWM or digital commands. A DAC alone normally cannot supply motor power. Mechanical limits, response time and feedback all affect whether an intended action is achieved.

blocks.title: Human-AI interaction is part of HCI
blocks.text: Human-computer interaction studies how people use computing systems. Human-AI interaction focuses on challenges raised by AI, including uncertainty, adaptation, delegation and trust. It is not a strict division between deterministic old interfaces and always-probabilistic new ones. The important question is what the person needs to understand and control.

blocks.title: Useful interface information
rows: The user knows what the system is doing.
The user can judge an output appropriately.
The next behaviour is less surprising.
The user can respond when the system cannot continue.

blocks.title: Avoid over-trust and under-trust
blocks.text: Unclear automation can cause misuse through excessive reliance, or disuse when useful assistance is rejected. A handover should communicate the state of the task and why control is changing. A confident-looking score is not enough: the interface should support an informed decision and an appropriate human response.

blocks.title: Three important ethical concerns
rows: Who benefits, who is disadvantaged, and how was this measured?
Can affected people understand the system’s role and limitations?
Who is responsible for deployment, oversight and correction?

blocks.title: Reward design can encode priorities
blocks.text: A reward that values only throughput can encourage neglect of other goals. Historical data can contain unequal representation or biased decisions. Evaluate outcomes across relevant groups and situations rather than assuming an algorithm is neutral because it uses numbers. The appropriate criteria depend on the task and the people affected.

blocks.title: Make responsibility practical
blocks.text: Document the intended use, data sources, limitations and monitoring process. Provide channels to question or correct consequential outcomes. Ethical and legal requirements vary by context and jurisdiction; no single checklist proves a system is responsible. For high-stakes uses, performance testing and meaningful human oversight are essential parts of the deployment decision.

blocks.title: Measure outcomes, not just activity
blocks.text: More sensor readings or more automated actions do not necessarily mean better service. Compare meaningful outcomes such as resource use, reliability, accessibility and user experience. Any claimed improvement needs evidence from the particular deployment; percentages from an unspecified example are not general guarantees.

blocks.title: Every connected device adds responsibilities
blocks.text: Connected cameras, locks, sensors and controllers need updates, access management and appropriate data protection. Minimise unnecessary personal data, limit retention and protect communication. Consider what happens if a device is compromised or the network is unavailable. Convenience should be assessed alongside maintainability, privacy and safe operation.

blocks.title: Build your vocabulary
rows: Hardware, communication and software integrated for a useful task.
Processing that must satisfy a specified timing deadline.
Technology performing some or all parts of a task with reduced direct human operation.
Processing near the source / processing on remote shared infrastructure.
Interaction challenges involving AI, including uncertainty, delegation and trust.
Design and use that consider fairness, accountability, transparency and impacts on people.
The conditions under which a system is intended to function.
Measurements and status information communicated for monitoring or analysis.

blocks.title: Strengths and limitations interact
rows: Power, heat, memory and physical reliability.
Selects actions and may learn from experience.
Model errors, limited evidence and unclear objectives.

blocks.title: There is no universally best architecture
blocks.text: Choose a design for its task, operating conditions and consequences of failure. A model with excellent offline accuracy may be unsuitable if it misses a deadline or requires too much memory. A highly connected system may be fragile if local operation depends on one remote service. A simple fixed-rule controller can be appropriate for a well-defined task.

blocks.title: Make the comparison explicit
blocks.text: State the intended outcome, identify constraints, compare options and define measures for success. Evaluate the combination of hardware, networking, algorithms and human operation. A component’s specification is useful evidence, but it is not proof that the complete application meets its requirements.

blocks.title: Every device has limits
blocks.caption: A design must fit all four budgets, not just the model’s arithmetic requirement.

blocks.title: Understand the constraint
rows: A battery drains too quickly for the required mission.
Weights, inputs or intermediate results do not fit.
An inference or control computation misses its deadline.

blocks.title: Optimise with evidence
blocks.text: A smaller model, quantised representation, reduced input resolution or lower update rate can reduce cost, but may change accuracy or responsiveness. Measure the resulting behaviour. Dedicated accelerators can improve efficiency on supported workloads, but data conversion, memory movement and idle power remain relevant. Local computing removes a remote round trip; it does not mean zero total latency.

blocks.title: Sensors are imperfect
blocks.text: Noise creates random variation; drift changes a sensor’s behaviour over time. Obstruction, calibration error or environmental conditions can produce misleading observations. Sensor fusion combines information from multiple sources, often after time alignment and filtering. Different sensors can have complementary strengths, but they can also share common failure causes.

blocks.title: A fusion pipeline
blocks.caption: Do not combine incompatible units or measurements from different times as if they described the same instant.

blocks.title: Define reliability under conditions
blocks.text: Reliability concerns performing an intended function for a stated period under stated conditions. MTBF is a statistical measure for repairable systems, not a promise that a particular unit cannot fail earlier. Monitor drift, error rates, temperature and data quality. Redundancy can help when failures are sufficiently independent and the system can recognise and manage disagreement.

blocks.title: Three network qualities
rows: Handle more devices or work at acceptable performance.
Exchange data and use it correctly across different systems.
Maintain or recover an acceptable service during disruption.

blocks.title: Capacity is only one part of scaling
blocks.text: Adding hundreds of IoT devices can increase addressing, authentication, message traffic, storage and maintenance work. Agree on data formats, units, timestamps and interface versions as well as the physical link. Two products using Wi-Fi do not automatically interpret one another’s messages correctly.

blocks.title: Plan for failures
blocks.text: Redundant links, retry policies, local buffering and controlled reconnection can improve resilience. A mesh can route around some failures when an alternative path exists and the protocols support it. It does not guarantee communication through every outage. Test overload and partial failure, not just the normal case with every device online.

title: Put each computation where it fits

blocks.title: Three deployment patterns
rows: Another service to size and manage.
Network dependency, latency and transfer cost.

blocks.title: An illustrative warehouse design
blocks.text: Each robot handles immediate motion control locally. A shared service allocates tasks and coordinates inventory. Robots send selected telemetry and receive authorised updates. If the coordination service is unavailable, the design defines whether a robot pauses, completes a limited task or enters another safe state; continued operation must not be assumed.

blocks.title: Optimise across the whole path
blocks.text: Compare local compute energy with transmission energy, available bandwidth, deadlines, privacy and model capacity. Summarising data locally can reduce transfer volume. Centralised analysis can reveal patterns across devices. The useful decision is which part of the workload belongs where, not whether edge or cloud is always superior.

title: Predict an outcome or model behaviour?

blocks.title: Two useful questions
rows: How does an agent or system behave?
Rules, transitions, trajectories or action patterns.
Example: estimate a component’s failure risk.
Example: model a robot’s response to an obstacle.

blocks.title: The approaches can overlap
blocks.text: A behavioural model can be used to make predictions, and predictive features can inform an action policy. They are not mutually exclusive categories defined by one kind of data. Choose the model and evaluation method based on the question being asked and the evidence available.

blocks.title: Adaptation is not guaranteed generalisation
blocks.text: Adaptive intelligence describes changing behaviour appropriately using new information or experience. Autonomy describes operating with limited direct human control. An autonomous device may use a fixed policy; an adaptive model may still need supervision. Performance in familiar conditions does not prove reliability in a new environment.

blocks.title: Explainability is a practical capability
blocks.text: Explainability concerns making relevant aspects of a model’s behaviour understandable to people. A small rule set or Q table may be inspectable. A deep RL policy can be harder to interpret because many parameters contribute to each output. Complexity does not mean analysis is impossible, but a simple story about one decision may be incomplete or misleading.

blocks.title: Look beyond one successful outcome
blocks.text: Inspect representative cases, counterexamples, changed conditions and failure logs. Separate a faithful explanation of the computation from a plausible narrative generated after the fact. An explanation does not establish that the action was correct; validation requires evidence about outcomes and requirements.

blocks.title: Reward errors and bias
blocks.text: An agent rewarded only for speed may neglect an important constraint. Training environments can under-represent some conditions or groups. Distribution shift can reduce performance when deployment differs from training. Track both overall performance and relevant subsets. Correcting a reward or dataset requires re-evaluation of the resulting policy.

blocks.title: Questions for a deployment review
rows: Authenticated updates, restricted access and recovery plans.
Necessary data collection, appropriate retention and access.
Evaluation across relevant people and conditions.
Named responsibilities, review and correction routes.
Measured deadlines, failure handling and monitoring.

blocks.title: Physical effects raise the stakes
blocks.text: A connected controller can change the physical world, so a corrupted measurement or unauthorised command may have consequences beyond a damaged file. Protect sensor inputs, model updates and actuator commands according to the task. Test how the system responds to missing, stale and contradictory data.

blocks.title: Finish with a justified judgement
blocks.text: State the benefit you expect, the evidence supporting it, the conditions under which it applies and the remaining limitations. Decide what a human must monitor or approve and how the system should respond when its assumptions fail. The strongest design is the one suited to its purpose, with limitations that are understood and managed.

blocks.title: Build your vocabulary
rows: Connecting and coordinating measurements for a computing system.
Limits such as power, thermal capacity, memory and compute time.
Performance of the intended function over time under stated conditions.
A gradual change in measurement behaviour or calibration.
Ability to handle growth at acceptable performance.
Ability to exchange information and use it correctly across systems.
Ability to maintain or recover acceptable service through disruption.
Balancing computation, communication, energy and other costs for a goal.
Changing behaviour appropriately using new information or experience.

blocks.title: How to read this edition
blocks.text: Page numbers refer to physical PDF pages, including the cover and dividers. Each teaching or reference page ends with a question from the team’s exercise files. The complete Stage 2 edition includes six missions, resources and explained answers after the core chapters. Wording is lightly edited for clarity and technical accuracy. Worked examples teach methods using separate examples. The original art’s printed chapter labels determine the divider order.
